scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance emerged in the late 1980s in Melbourne's underground rave scene.
It was initially known by various names including 'stomping' or 'rocking'.
The term 'Melbourne shuffle' was popularized in the 1990s by media and visitors, eventually becoming the standard name.
on_screen: Map: Australia · Oceania
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a club and rave dance, it is rooted in the PLUR (Peace, Love, Unity, Respect) philosophy.
It serves as a form of self-expression and is now performed in festivals, clubs, and on social media platforms.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Crawford High School The Art of Shuffling (https://archive.org/details/macsdca-Crawford_High_School_The_Art_of_Shuffling)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance relies on the T-step (a pivot-based heel-toe movement) and the running man (a sliding jump sequence).
Arms move in coordination with the feet, either side-to-side or vertically.
Improvisation is central, with dancers adding spins, kicks, and slides to match the tempo.
Watch for T-step, Running man.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (eeAzwFkfyPA)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Typically solo improvisation, moving within a small area.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to electronic dance music, specifically genres like acid house, trance, hardstyle, and hard dance.
Tempos are typically fast, ranging from 130 to 150 BPM.
Listen for the Synthesizers, Drum machines.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 140 beats a minute.
Fast-paced, repetitive electronic beats with heavy basslines and synthesized melodies characteristic of rave music.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Historically, dancers often wore 'phat pants'—wide-legged trousers that helped hide footwork and allowed for airflow.
Dancers frequently use talcum powder or liquid on the floor to facilitate sliding.
on_screen: Images — MISSING
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Rupert Keiller is credited with helping popularize the term 'Melbourne shuffle' on Australian television.
Dancers Pae (Missaghi Peyman) and Sarah Miatt are noted for their appearances in the music video for Scooter's 'J'adore Hardcore'.
A related style known as 'cutting shapes' developed in the United Kingdom and the Netherlands by 2012, which differs in technique and history from the Melbourne shuffle.
The dance shares similarities with earlier jazz dance styles and has been influenced by the rave culture of the 1980s and 1990s.
